nodes.name: tau-inequality of at most 4 terms
nodes.statement: This motivates us to study a system of inequalities whose left-hand side consists of at most 4 terms (non-negative integers or constants) and whose right-hand side is $\tau$. We call such an inequality a {\it $\tau$-inequality of at most 4 terms}; we use this term often with the replacement of $\tau$ by either $\ge_\tau$ (at least $\tau$) or $<_\tau$ (strictly less than $\tau$) to specify its sign.
nodes.statement_short: An inequality with at most 4 nonnegative-integer terms on the left and $\tau$ on the right; written $\ge_\tau$ or $<_\tau$ by sign.

nodes.name: tile complexity
nodes.statement: There and also in this paper, the optimality of TASs is measured by the number of distinct tile types they contain, and this criterion is called the {\it tile complexity}.
differentia: the number of distinct tile types they contain

nodes.name: $\Sigma^*$
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma$ be an alphabet, and by $\Sigma^*$, we denote the set of finite strings over $\Sigma$.

nodes.name: $\mathbb{N}_0$
nodes.statement: By $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{N}$, we denote the set of integers and the set of positive integers, respectively, and let $\mathbb{N}_0 = \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}$.

nodes.name: full grid graph
nodes.statement: Given a set of points $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2$ on the integer lattice, the {\it full grid graph} of $A$ is the undirected graph $G^{\rm f}_A = (V, E)$, where $V = A$ and for all $u, v \in V$, there is an edge between $u$ and $v$ if and only if $||u-v||_2 = 1$, where $|| \cdot ||_2$ is the Manhattan distance, that is, $u$ and $v$ are adjacent points.
differentia: there is an edge between $u$ and $v$ if and only if $||u-v||_2 = 1$

nodes.name: shape
nodes.statement: A {\it shape} is a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2$ such that $G^{\rm f}_S$ is connected, and we denote the set of all {\it finite} shapes by $\mathcal{FS} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{Z}^2)$.

nodes.name: directions N, W, S, E
nodes.statement: Let ${\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}$ stand for the respective directions north, west, south, and east, and be also interpreted as the respective unit vectors $(0, 1), (-1, 0), (0, -1), (1, 0)$.

nodes.name: tile type
nodes.statement: A {\it tile type} $t$ is a quadruple $t \in \Sigma^* \times \Sigma^* \times \Sigma^* \times \Sigma^*$, and is regarded as a unit square with four sides listed in the counter-clockwise order starting at the north ({\tt N}), each having a {\it glue label} (a.k.a., {\it glue}) taken from $\Sigma^*$.
nodes.statement_short: A tile type is a unit square whose four sides (N, W, S, E) each carry a glue label from $\Sigma^*$.

nodes.name: $t(d)$
nodes.statement: For each direction $d \in \{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\}$, let $t(d)$ be the glue label at the $d$ side of $t$.

nodes.name: $\Lambda(T)$
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a {\it finite} set of tile types, and let us denote the (finite) set of all glues of tile types in $T$ by $\Lambda(T) \subsetneq \Sigma^*$.

nodes.name: assembly
nodes.statement: An {\it assembly} (a.k.a., {\it supertile}) is a positioning of tiles of types in $T$ on (part of) the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$. It does not have to be a tessellation. Hence, we can say that an assembly is a partial function $\mathbb{Z}^2 \dashrightarrow T$.

nodes.name: sub-assembly
nodes.statement: Given two assemblies $\alpha, \beta: \mathbb{Z}^2 \dashrightarrow T$, $\alpha$ is a {\it sub-assembly} of $\beta$, written as $\alpha \sqsubseteq \beta$, if $\ensuremath{\mathrm{dom}}(\alpha) \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathrm{dom}}(\beta)$ and for every point $p \in \ensuremath{\mathrm{dom}}(\alpha)$, $\alpha(p) = \beta(p)$, where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{dom}}$ denotes the domain of the function.

nodes.name: strength function
nodes.statement: A {\it strength function $g: \Lambda(T) \to \mathbb{N}_0$} endows tiles with an ability to interact with its neighboring tiles by assigning the strength $g(\ell)$ to the {\it matching} label $\ell$ of their abutting edges. If the labels do not match or $g(\ell) = 0$, these tiles do not interact; otherwise, they do.

nodes.name: binding graph
nodes.statement: An assembly $\alpha$ and a strength function $g$ induce a {\it binding graph}, which is a grid graph whose vertices are $\ensuremath{\mathrm{dom}}(\alpha)$ and for two neighboring positions $p_1, p_2 \in \ensuremath{\mathrm{dom}}(\alpha)$, there is an edge between $p_1$ and $p_2$ on this graph if and only if the tiles $\alpha(p_1)$ and $\alpha(p_2)$ interact. On this graph, an edge between vertices means that the corresponding tiles interact, and hence, their abutting edges share the same label $\ell$. Thus, we can consider that the edge is labeled with $\ell$ and $g$ gives it the weight $g(\ell)$.
nodes.statement_short: Grid graph on the assembly's positions with an edge, weighted $g(\ell)$, between neighbouring tiles that interact.

nodes.name: tau-stable assembly
nodes.statement: The assembly is {\it $\tau$-stable (with respect to $g$)} if every cut of its binding graph has strength at least $\tau$. That is, the assembly is $\tau$-stable if at least energy $\tau$ is required to separate it into two parts.
differentia: every cut of its binding graph has strength at least $\tau$

nodes.name: tile assembly system (TAS)
nodes.statement: A {\it (seeded) tile assembly system} (TAS) is a quadruple $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}} = (T, \sigma, g, \tau)$, where $T$ and $g$ are as stated above, $\sigma: \mathbb{Z}^2 \dashrightarrow T$ is a finite $\tau$-stable {\it seed assembly}, and $\tau \ge 1$ is an integer parameter called {\it temperature}.
nodes.statement_short: A TAS is $(T,\sigma,g,\tau)$: tile types, a finite $\tau$-stable seed, a strength function and an integer temperature $\tau\ge 1$.

nodes.name: tile
nodes.statement: TASs are provided with inexhaustible supply of copies of each tile type, each copy being referred to as a {\it tile}.

nodes.name: singly-seeded TAS
nodes.statement: If the seed assembly $\sigma$ consists of a single tile, then $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ is said to be {\it singly-seeded}.

nodes.name: only singly-seeded TASs
nodes.statement: In this paper, we consider only singly-seeded TASs.

nodes.name: T-produces in one step
nodes.statement: Given two $\tau$-stable assemblies $\alpha, \beta$, we write $\alpha \to_1^{\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}} \beta$ if $\alpha \sqsubseteq \beta$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{dom}}(\beta) \setminus \ensuremath{\mathrm{dom}}(\alpha) = \{p\}$ for some position $p \in \mathbb{Z}^2$. Intuitively, this means that $\alpha$ can grow into $\beta$ by the addition of a single tile at the position $p$. Since $\beta$ is required to be $\tau$-stable, the new tile is able to bind to $\alpha$ with strength at least $\tau$. In this case, we say that {\it $\alpha$ $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$-produces $\beta$ in one step}.
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha$ grows into $\tau$-stable $\beta$ by adding a single tile.

nodes.name: T-assembly sequence
nodes.statement: A sequence of $\tau$-stable assemblies $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_k$ is a {\it $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$-assembly sequence} if for all $1 \le i \le k$, $\alpha_{i-1} \to_1^{\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}} \alpha_i$ holds.

nodes.name: T-produces
nodes.statement: We write $\alpha \to^\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}} \beta$ and say {\it $\alpha$ $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$-produces $\beta$} (in 0 or more steps) if there is a $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$-assembly sequence $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_k$ of length $k = |\ensuremath{\mathrm{dom}}(\beta) \setminus \ensuremath{\mathrm{dom}}(\alpha)|$ with $\alpha_0 = \alpha$ and $\alpha_k = \beta$.

nodes.name: producible assembly
nodes.statement: An assembly $\alpha$ is {\it $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$-producible} or {\it producible by $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$} if $\sigma \to^\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}} \alpha$.

nodes.name: terminal assembly
nodes.statement: A $\tau$-stable assembly $\alpha$ is {\it ($\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$-)terminal} if for any $\tau$-stable assembly $\beta$, $\alpha \to^\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}} \beta$ implies $\alpha = \beta$.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{A}[\mathcal{T}]$ and $\mathcal{A}_\Box[\mathcal{T}]$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{A}[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}]$ be the set of assemblies producible by $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$, and let $\mathcal{A}_\Box[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}] \subseteq \mathcal{A}[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}]$ be the set of terminal assemblies that are producible by $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$.

nodes.name: directed TAS
nodes.statement: A TAS $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ is {\it directed} if the poset $(\mathcal{A}[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}], \to^\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}})$ is directed, i.e., for each $\alpha, \beta \in \mathcal{A}[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}]$, there exists $\gamma \in \mathcal{A}[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}]$ such that $\alpha \to^\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}} \gamma$ and $\beta \to^\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}} \gamma$.

nodes.name: strictly self-assembles
nodes.statement: Given a shape $S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2$, a TAS $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ {\it strictly (a.k.a.,~uniquely) (self-)assembles} $S$ if the shape of every terminal assembly produced by $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ is $S$.

nodes.name: temperature-2 directed tile complexity
nodes.statement: The {\it temperature-2 directed tile complexity} of $S$ is formally defined as follows: \[ \dtilec{2}(S) = \min \biggl\{|T| \left| \begin{array}{r} \mbox{$\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}} = (T, \sigma, g, 2)$ is a directed TAS} \\ \mbox{that strictly self-assembles $S$} \end{array} \right\}. \] This is the minimum number of tile types required for a directed TAS at the temperature 2 to strictly self-assemble $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimum number of tile types of a directed temperature-2 TAS that strictly self-assembles $S$.

nodes.name: temperature-1 TASs are covered at temperature 2
nodes.statement: Since any temperature-1 TAS can be simulated at the temperature 2 simply by doubling the strength associated to each of its labels (see also Proposition~\ref{prop:simulation_at_high_temp}), this definition indeed has already taken the temperature-1 TASs into account.

nodes.name: directed tile complexity at temperature tau
nodes.statement: We parameterize this complexity measure by a temperature $\tau$ as: \[ \dtilec{\tau}(S) = \min \biggl\{|T| \left| \begin{array}{r} \mbox{$\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}} = (T, \sigma, g, \tau)$ is a directed TAS} \\ \mbox{that strictly self-assembles $S$} \end{array} \right\}, \] and introduce it as {\it directed tile complexity of $S$ at the temperature $\tau$}.
nodes.statement_short: Minimum number of tile types of a directed temperature-$\tau$ TAS that strictly self-assembles $S$.

nodes.name: temperature-1 complexity dominates temperature-2
nodes.statement: As mentioned above, $\dtilec{1}(S) \ge \dtilec{2}(S)$ for any $S$.
conclusions: $\dtilec{1}(S) \ge \dtilec{2}(S)$ for any $S$

nodes.name: complexity non-increasing under multiplying the temperature
nodes.statement: Now we show that for any temperature $\tau$ and a positive integer $k$, $\dtilec{\tau}(S) \ge \dtilec{k\tau}(S)$ holds.
assumptions: for any temperature $\tau$ and a positive integer $k$
conclusions: $\dtilec{\tau}(S) \ge \dtilec{k\tau}(S)$ holds

nodes.name: Simulation at high temperatures
nodes.statement: For any $\tau \in \mathbb{N}$, TASs at the temperature $\tau$ can be simulated at any temperature that is a multiple of $\tau$.
conclusions: TASs at the temperature $\tau$ can be simulated at any temperature that is a multiple of $\tau$
nodes.label: prop:simulation_at_high_temp

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: This simulation is simply done by multiplying the strengths and $\tau$ of a given TAS $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_1 = (T, \sigma, g, \tau)$ by a proper constant $c$. The TAS thus obtained is $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_2 = (T, \sigma, g', c\tau)$ with $g'(\ell) = c g(\ell)$ for each glue label $\ell$ in $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply all glue strengths and the temperature by the same constant $c$.

nodes.name: non-monotonicity of directed tile complexity
nodes.statement: Neither this proposition nor Theorem~\ref{thm:tau_better_than_less} in Section~\ref{sec:complexity} implies the monotonically decreasing property of $\dtilec{\tau}(S)$, being considered as a function of $\tau$. Indeed, it is not so as being exemplified at the end of Section~\ref{sec:complexity}.

nodes.name: directed tile complexity at temperatures at most tau
nodes.statement: This non-monotonicity motivates us to introduce the notion of {\it directed tile complexity of $S$ at the temperatures at most $\tau$}. This measure is to be defined as \[ \dtilec{\le \tau}(S) = \min\{\dtilec{i}(S) \mid 1 \le i \le \tau\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: $\dtilec{\le \tau}(S)$ is the minimum of $\dtilec{i}(S)$ over temperatures $1 \le i \le \tau$.

nodes.name: locally identical behaviours of TASs
nodes.statement: As the TASs $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_1$ and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_2$ in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:simulation_at_high_temp}, more than one TAS can exhibit identical behaviors at the local (attachment) level in the sense that whenever some of the four sides of a tile cooperate for the stable attachment in one TAS, a tile of the same type do so in the other TASs, though these TAS may be at different temperatures and may assign each label with different strengths. As a result, they produce the same shapes.
nodes.statement_short: Different TASs, possibly at different temperatures, can behave identically per attachment and hence produce the same shapes.

nodes.name: cooperation set
nodes.statement: More precisely, $g$ and $\tau$ do so by specifying the local behavior of each tile type $t \in T$ in the form of {\it cooperation set of $t$ with respect to $g$ and $\tau$} \cite{ChenDotySeki2011}, which is defined as: \[ \mathcal{D}_{g, \tau}(t) = \Bigl\{ D \subseteq \{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\} \Bigm| \mbox{$\sum_{d \in D} g(t(d)) \ge \tau$} \Bigr\}. \] This is the collection of sets of four sides of $t$ whose glues have sufficient strengths to bind $t$ cooperatively.
nodes.definiendum: cooperation set of $t$ with respect to $g$ and $\tau$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{D}_{g,\tau}(t)$ is the family of side sets of $t$ whose glue strengths sum to at least $\tau$.

nodes.name: cooperation sets are upward closed
nodes.statement: By definition, if a set of sides of $t$ is in $\mathcal{D}_{g, \tau}(t)$, then any of its superset is also included in $\mathcal{D}_{g, \tau}(t)$.
assumptions: if a set of sides of $t$ is in $\mathcal{D}_{g, \tau}(t)$
conclusions: then any of its superset is also included in $\mathcal{D}_{g, \tau}(t)$

nodes.name: full side set in every cooperation set
nodes.statement: Any tile type whose cooperation set is empty can be rid from $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ because a tile of that type never attaches. Combining these together, we assume that for any $t \in T$, $\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\} \in \mathcal{D}_{g, \tau}(t)$.

nodes.name: locally equivalent TASs
nodes.statement: Given $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_1 = (T, \sigma, g_1, \tau_1)$ and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_2 = (T, \sigma, g_2, \tau_2)$ that share the tile set $T$ and seed $\sigma$, if $\mathcal{D}_{g_1, \tau_1}(t) = \mathcal{D}_{g_2, \tau_2}(t)$ for each tile type $t \in T$, then these TASs are said to be {\it locally equivalent} (written as $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_1 \sim \ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_2$) \cite{ChenDotySeki2011}.
nodes.statement_short: Two TASs with the same tiles and seed are locally equivalent if every tile type has the same cooperation set in both.

nodes.name: Argument that locally equivalent TASs produce the same assemblies
nodes.statement: The behaviors of locally equivalent TASs are exactly the same at the tile attachment level. This easily leads us to the property that a sequence of assemblies $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_k$ is a $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_1$-assembly sequence if and only if it is a $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_2$-assembly sequence. From this it follows that these TASs produce the same assemblies as well as the same terminal assemblies.
nodes.statement_short: Identical attachment behaviour gives identical assembly sequences, hence identical (terminal) producible assemblies.

nodes.name: local equivalence preserves producible assemblies
nodes.statement: In short, $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_1 \sim \ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_2$ implies $\mathcal{A}[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_1] = \mathcal{A}[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_2]$ and $\mathcal{A}_\Box[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_1] = \mathcal{A}_\Box[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_2]$.
conclusions: $\mathcal{A}[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_1] = \mathcal{A}[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_2]$
$\mathcal{A}_\Box[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_1] = \mathcal{A}_\Box[\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_2]$

nodes.name: Local equivalence preserves directedness and strict self-assembly
nodes.statement: As a corollary, we can see that given locally equivalent TASs, one is directed and strictly self-assembles a shape if and only if so is and does the other.
conclusions: one is directed and strictly self-assembles a shape if and only if so is and does the other

nodes.name: behaviour of a local-equivalence class
nodes.statement: The local equivalence $\sim$ divides the set of all TASs into the equivalence classes. All the TASs in a resulting equivalence class behave exactly in the same way locally, and hence, we are allowed to use the term ``behavior of this class.'' This means that the class can choose a TAS $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}} = (T, \sigma, g, \tau)$ it contains arbitrarily as representative in describing its behavior by the pair $(T, \{\mathcal{D}_{g, \tau}(t) \mid t \in T\})$. This suggests a way to define a variant of TAS by assigning each $t \in T$ with a set of subsets of $\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\}$ as a cooperation set.
nodes.statement_short: Local equivalence classes have a well-defined behaviour, described by the tile set and cooperation sets of any representative.

nodes.name: strength-free TAS
nodes.statement: Chen, Doty, and Seki introduced this variant called {\it strength-free TAS} \cite{ChenDotySeki2011} as it is free from strength function or temperature. Formally, a {\it strength-free TAS} is a triple $(T, \sigma, \mathcal{D})$, where $T$ and $\sigma$ are the same as those for TAS, while $\mathcal{D}: T \to \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\}))$ is a function from a tile type $t \in T$ to a set of subsets of $\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\}$ that is closed under superset operation, where $\mathcal{P}$ means the power set.
differentia: $\mathcal{D}: T \to \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\}))$ is a function from a tile type $t \in T$ to a set of subsets of $\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\}$ that is closed under superset operation
nodes.statement_short: A TAS variant that assigns each tile type an upward-closed cooperation set directly, with no strengths or temperature.

nodes.name: local equivalence of a TAS and a strength-free TAS
nodes.statement: As done between TASs, we can define the local equivalence between a TAS $(T, \sigma, g, \tau)$ and a strength-free TAS $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_{\rm sf} = (T, \sigma, \mathcal{D})$ as: they are {\it locally-equivalent} if $\mathcal{D}(t) = \mathcal{D}_{g, \tau}(t)$ for each $t \in T$.

nodes.name: strength-free representative is class-invariant
nodes.statement: For an equivalence class, if $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_{\rm sf}$ is locally equivalent to an element of the class, then so is it to all of them.
assumptions: if $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_{\rm sf}$ is locally equivalent to an element of the class
conclusions: then so is it to all of them

nodes.name: uniqueness of the representing strength-free TAS
nodes.statement: Of particular note is that such a strength-free TAS is unique for each class.
conclusions: such a strength-free TAS is unique for each class

nodes.name: non-implementable strength-free TASs exist
nodes.statement: It must be also noted that there exists a strength-free TAS that does not represent any class, that is, that is not locally equivalent to any TAS.
conclusions: there exists a strength-free TAS that does not represent any class

nodes.name: FindStrength
nodes.statement: This implementability check was formalized as $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc FindStrength}}$ in \cite{ChenDotySeki2011}, which is defined as follows: \[ \begin{array}{l} \ensuremath{\mbox{\sc FindStrength}} \\ \begin{array}{ll} {\tt INPUT:} & \mbox{a strength-free TAS $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_{\rm sf}$} \\ {\tt OUTPUT:} & \mbox{a TAS that is locally equivalent to $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_{\rm sf}$, if any,}\\ & \mbox{or reports that none of such TAS exists otherwise}. \end{array} \end{array} \]
nodes.statement_short: Given a strength-free TAS, output a locally equivalent TAS or report that none exists.

nodes.name: FindStrength is polynomial-time solvable
nodes.statement: A polynomial-time algorithm for this problem was proposed in \cite{ChenDotySeki2011}.
conclusions: A polynomial-time algorithm for this problem

nodes.name: Adleman et al. minimum directed temperature-2 TAS algorithm for squares
nodes.statement: In the paper, they proposed an algorithm to find a minimum size directed TAS $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}} = (T, \sigma, g, 2)$ that strictly self-assembles the $n \times n$ square $\square{n}$, subject to the constraint that the TAS's temperature is 2. Note that $\dtilec{2}(\square{n}) = O(\frac{\log n}{\log \log n})$ \cite{AdChGoHu2001}. This algorithm enumerates all temperature-2 TASs with at most $\dtilec{2}(\square{n})$ tile types, and checks whether each of them is directed and strictly self-assembles $\square{n}$ (this is proved to be polynomial-time checkable in $n$). The temperature of a system to be checked need not be 2, but rather the temperature-2 restriction\footnote{This can be replaced with the temperature-$c$ restriction for any constant $c \ge 1$.} is utilized to upper-bound the number of all candidates to be thus checked by a polynomial in $n$, and as a result, this algorithm runs in a polynomial time in $n$.
output: a minimum size directed TAS $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}} = (T, \sigma, g, 2)$ that strictly self-assembles the $n \times n$ square $\square{n}$
nodes.statement_short: Enumerate all temperature-2 TASs with at most $\dtilec{2}(\square{n})$ tile types and test each for directed strict self-assembly of $\square{n}$.

nodes.name: Removing the temperature bound in the minimum square TAS algorithm
nodes.statement: The open problem was whether the temperature upper-bound could be removed.

nodes.name: Chen-Doty-Seki polynomial-time algorithm without temperature bound
nodes.statement: Chen, Doty, and Seki answered this problem positively by designing an algorithm that runs in polynomial time in $n$ without relying on such an upper-bound \cite{ChenDotySeki2011}.
conclusions: an algorithm that runs in polynomial time in $n$ without relying on such an upper-bound

nodes.name: Chen-Doty-Seki strength-free enumeration algorithm
nodes.statement: Though being based on the above-mentioned idea by Adleman et al.~basically, their algorithm enumerates strength-free TASs with at most $\dtilec{2}(\square{n})$ tile types instead of conventional ones, and commits extra check for the implementability.
nodes.statement_short: Enumerate strength-free TASs with at most $\dtilec{2}(\square{n})$ tile types and additionally check implementability.

nodes.name: Lowest-temperature minimum TAS for squares
nodes.statement: This algorithm raised another problem of whether it could be modified so as to output among all the minimum size directed TASs for $\square{n}$ the one(s) working at the lowest temperature.

nodes.name: FindOptimalStrength
nodes.statement: This motivates us to study the following optimization: \[ \begin{array}{l} \ensuremath{\mbox{\sc FindOptimalStrength}} \\ \begin{array}{ll} {\tt INPUT:} & \mbox{a strength-free TAS $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_{\rm sf}$} \\ {\tt OUTPUT:} & \mbox{a TAS of minimal temperature that is locally equivalent to $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}_{\rm sf}$} \\ & \mbox{if any, or reports that none of such TAS exists otherwise}. \end{array} \end{array} \]
nodes.statement_short: Given a strength-free TAS, output a locally equivalent TAS of minimal temperature, or report none exists.

nodes.name: Threshold programming (TP)
nodes.statement: In order to prove the {\tt NP}-hardness of $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc FindOptimalStrength}}$, let us introduce a subclass of integer programming (IP) that aims at optimizing $\tau$ subject to only $\ge_\tau$-inequalities and $<_\tau$-inequalities. We call such an IP a {\it threshold programming} (TP). This is formalized as: for given integer matrices $C_1, C_2$, minimize $\tau$ on condition that there exists a nonnegative integer vector $\Vec{x}$ satisfying \[ \mbox{$C_1 \vec{x} \ge \tau \Vec{1}$ ($\ge_\tau$-inequalities) and $C_2 \vec{x} < \tau \Vec{1}$ ($<_\tau$-inequalities)}, \] where $\Vec{1}$ is the vector all of whose components are 1.
nodes.statement_short: Integer program minimizing $\tau$ subject to $C_1 x \ge \tau\mathbf{1}$ and $C_2 x < \tau\mathbf{1}$ over nonnegative integer $x$.

nodes.name: FindOptimalStrength is a TP(4,3)
nodes.statement: $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc FindOptimalStrength}}$ is actually a TP any of whose constraints is either a $\ge_\tau$-inequality of at most 4 terms or a $<_\tau$-inequality of at most 3 terms.
conclusions: $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc FindOptimalStrength}}$ is actually a TP any of whose constraints is either a $\ge_\tau$-inequality of at most 4 terms or a $<_\tau$-inequality of at most 3 terms

nodes.name: Single-tile example showing FindOptimalStrength is a TP
nodes.statement: In order to see this, let us consider a simple strength-free TAS with only one tile type $t = (\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3, \ell_4)$ and a cooperation set $\mathcal{D}(t) = \{\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\}\}$. Finding a TAS at lowest temperature that is locally equivalent to this strength-free TAS is equal to solving the following system of inequalities with a {\it positive integer} variable $\tau$: \begin{equation} \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} \ell_1 + \ell_2 + \ell_3 + \ell_4 &\ge& \tau \\ \ell_1 + \ell_2 + \ell_3 &<& \tau \\ \ell_1 + \ell_2 + \ell_4 &<& \tau \\ \ell_1 + \ell_3 + \ell_4 &<& \tau \\ \ell_2 + \ell_3 + \ell_4 &<& \tau \\ \end{array} \right. \end{equation} so as to minimize $\tau$. The minimum $\tau$ for this system is 4 with $\ell_1 = \ell_2 = \ell_3 = \ell_4 = 1$ (with $\tau$ being strictly less than 4, this system is not solvable). The first inequality in \eqref{eq:TP_example_1} corresponds to $\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\} \in \mathcal{D}(t)$, the second corresponds to $\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}\} \not\in \mathcal{D}(t)$, and so forth. Though \eqref{eq:TP_example_1} does not seem to contain an inequality corresponding to $\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}\} \not\in \mathcal{D}(t)$, the second one (or third) actually implies this, and hence, not presented for the sake of space. In any case, the system for a cooperation set contains at most 15 inequalities.
nodes.statement_short: Write the cooperation set of a single tile as a system of $\ge_\tau$ and $<_\tau$ inequalities in its glue strengths; at most 15 arise.

nodes.name: Equation (1): single-tile threshold system
nodes.statement: \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} \ell_1 + \ell_2 + \ell_3 + \ell_4 &\ge& \tau \\ \ell_1 + \ell_2 + \ell_3 &<& \tau \\ \ell_1 + \ell_2 + \ell_4 &<& \tau \\ \ell_1 + \ell_3 + \ell_4 &<& \tau \\ \ell_2 + \ell_3 + \ell_4 &<& \tau \\ \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: eq:TP_example_1

nodes.name: TP(4,3)
nodes.statement: We denote the class of TPs any of whose constraints contains at most the number of terms as specified above by TP(4,~3).

nodes.name: tau-ThresholdProgramming(4,3)
nodes.statement: Its decision variant, denoted by $\tau$-$\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc ThresholdProgramming}}(4, 3)$ or simply $\tau$-TP(4,~3), is of interest in which $\tau$ is not a variable but a given constant, and one is asked to decide whether $\Vec{x}$ exists.
nodes.statement_short: Decision version of TP(4,3) for a fixed constant $\tau$: does a feasible $x$ exist?

nodes.name: Equation (2): positivity gadget
nodes.statement: x_1 + x_a \ge \tau \mbox{ and } x_a < \tau.
nodes.label: eq:positive

nodes.name: positivity gadget forces $x_1 \ge 1$
nodes.statement: This pair implies $x_1 \ge 1$.

nodes.name: positive variable
nodes.statement: In the rest, when we say that a system has a positive variable $x$, we assume that its positiveness is guaranteed in this way.

nodes.name: 2^{i+1}-adder
nodes.statement: Let us build a sub-system called {\it $2^{i+1}$-adder (to the lower bound of a variable)}. Based on a variable $x$ with a lower bound $n$, i.e., $x \ge n$, it aims at creating another variable with a lower bound $n+2^{i+1}$. Using $5i{+}5$ positive integer variables $z_1, z_2, x_0, x_b, x_c, A_k, A_k', A_k'', B_k', B_k'' (1 \le k \le i)$, we design the $2^{i+1}$-adder as follows: for $2 \le j \le i$, \begin{equation} \begin{array}{llll} A_1' + B_1' + x_0, & A_1'' + B_1'' + x_0 &\ge& \tau, \\ A_1 + B_1' + x_0, & A_1' + B_1'' + x_0 &<& \tau, \\ A_{j-1} + B_j' + A_j', & A_{j-1} + B_j'' + A_j'' &\ge& \tau, \\ A_{j-1}'' + B_j' + A_j, & A_j' + B_j'' + A_{j-1}'' &<& \tau, \\ A_i'' + x_b, & z_1 + x_c &<& \tau, \\ z_1 + x_b, & z_2 + x_c &\ge& \tau. \end{array} \end{equation}
nodes.definiendum: $2^{i+1}$-adder (to the lower bound of a variable)
nodes.statement_short: A system of 3-term $\tau$-inequalities in $5i+5$ positive variables that raises a lower bound $x \ge n$ to $n+2^{i+1}$.

nodes.name: 2^{i+1}-adder lower bound
nodes.statement: This is actually a modification of a system of inequalities proposed in \cite{ChenDotySeki2011}, and as shown there all the inequalities of \eqref{eq:ChenDotySeki2011} but those on the last two lines imply \begin{equation} A_i'' \ge A_i + 2^{i+1}-2 \end{equation} for $1 \le k \le i$. The remaining four inequalities yield $z_1 \ge A_i''+1$ and $z_2 \ge z_1 + 1$ (in fact, they implement a $2^1$-adder). As a result, $z_2 \ge A_i + 2^{i+1}$.

nodes.name: adder forces large temperature
nodes.statement: Assume that we have a variable $x$ whose value is at least a positive integer $n$. By setting $x = A_i$, we can have $A_i$ in the $2^i$-adder assume not only be positive but be at least $n_1$. Then $z_2 \ge n + 2^{i+1}$. Combining \eqref{eq:recurrence_relation_on_Ai}, $z_1 \ge A_i''+1$, $z_1 + x_c < \tau$, $A_i \ge n$, and $x_b, x_c \ge 1$ deduces that $\tau$ must be at least $n + 2^{i+1}+1$.
assumptions: Assume that we have a variable $x$ whose value is at least a positive integer $n$.
conclusions: $\tau$ must be at least $n + 2^{i+1}+1$

nodes.name: adder solvable for large temperature
nodes.statement: It is important that for any $\tau \ge n+2^{i+1}+1$, this system can be solved as follows: \[ \begin{array}{l} A_i = n, x_0 = A_1 = \cdots = A_{i-1} = 1, \\ A_k' = 2^k, B_k' = \tau - A_k' -1, A_k'' = 2^{k+1}-1, B_k'' = \tau - A_k'' -1 \mbox{ for $1 \le k < i$}, \\ A_i' = n + 2^i -1, B_i' = \tau - A_i' -1, A_i'' = n + 2^{i+1}-2, B_i'' = \tau - A_i'' -1, \\ z_1 = n+2^{i+1}-1, z_2 = n+2^{i+1}, x_b = \tau - (n+2^{i+1}-1), x_c = \tau - (n+2^{i+1}). \end{array} \]
conclusions: this system can be solved as follows
nodes.statement_short: For every $\tau \ge n+2^{i+1}+1$ the adder has an explicit solution.

nodes.name: variables with arbitrarily large lower bounds
nodes.statement: With the fact that any positive number $m \ge 1$ can be written as a sum of powers of 2, this property makes possible to combine multiple copies of $2^{i+1}$-adders inductively in order to provide a variable with an arbitrarily large lower bound. The number of variables involved in the system thus built is at most $\sum_{i = 1}^{\lceil \log m \rceil} (5i+5)$, which is $O((\log m)^2)$.
assumptions: any positive number $m \ge 1$ can be written as a sum of powers of 2
conclusions: combine multiple copies of $2^{i+1}$-adders inductively in order to provide a variable with an arbitrarily large lower bound
The number of variables involved in the system thus built is at most $\sum_{i = 1}^{\lceil \log m \rceil} (5i+5)$, which is $O((\log m)^2)$.

nodes.name: adder is 3-term and four-partite
nodes.statement: Concerning \eqref{eq:ChenDotySeki2011}, the $2^{i+1}$-adder, there are two things to be noted. The first is that it consists of $\tau$-inequalities of at most three terms. The second is that we can divide its variables into four disjoint sets $V_1, V_2, V_3, V_4$ such that each inequality contains at most one variable from each of the four sets. One such division is: $V_1 = \{x_0, z_1, z_2\} \cup \{A_{2k}, A_{2k}', A_{2k}'' \mid 1 \le k \le \lfloor i/2 \rfloor\}$, $V_2 = \{A_{2k-1}, A_{2k-1}', A_{2k-1}'' \mid 1 \le k \le \lfloor i/2 \rfloor\}$, $V_3 = \{B_j, B_j', B_j'' \mid 1 \le j \le i\} \cup \{x_b, x_c\}$, and $V_4 = \emptyset$.
conclusions: it consists of $\tau$-inequalities of at most three terms
we can divide its variables into four disjoint sets $V_1, V_2, V_3, V_4$ such that each inequality contains at most one variable from each of the four sets

nodes.name: quadripartite system of tau-inequalities
nodes.statement: We say that a system of $\tau$-inequalities is {\it quadripartite} if \begin{enumerate} \item every inequality in it consists of at most {\it four} terms; \item its variable set can be partitioned into four disjoint subsets so that distinct terms of each inequality belong to distinct subsets. \end{enumerate}
differentia: every inequality in it consists of at most {\it four} terms
its variable set can be partitioned into four disjoint subsets so that distinct terms of each inequality belong to distinct subsets

nodes.name: monotone 1-in-3-SAT
nodes.statement: For the reduction, we employ a variant of 3-$\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}$ called monotone $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ introduced by Schaefer \cite{Schaefer1978}, in which no literal is negated (monotonicity) and one is required to find a truth assignment such that each clause has {\it exactly one} true literal.

nodes.name: Schaefer: monotone 1-in-3-SAT is NP-complete
nodes.statement: He proved its {\tt NP}-completeness.
conclusions: its {\tt NP}-completeness

nodes.name: quadripartite 1-in-3-SAT
nodes.statement: We propose its restricted variant called {\it quadripartite $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$}, whose instance consists of a variable set that is a union of four pairwise disjoint sets $U_1, U_2, U_3, U_4$ and clauses that contain at most one variable from each of these four subsets.
differentia: variable set that is a union of four pairwise disjoint sets $U_1, U_2, U_3, U_4$
clauses that contain at most one variable from each of these four subsets

nodes.name: Quadripartite 1-in-3-SAT is NP-complete
nodes.statement: Quadripartite $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ is {\tt NP}-complete.
conclusions: Quadripartite $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ is {\tt NP}-complete.
nodes.label: lem:quad_1in3SAT

nodes.statement_short: Reduce monotone 1-in-3-SAT clause by clause to a 13-clause gadget, then apply a quadripartizing clause conversion. Satisfiability preservation is checked by case analysis on $x,y,z$.

nodes.name: tau-ThresholdProgramming(4,3) is NP-complete
nodes.statement: For any $\tau \ge 4$, $\tau$-$\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc ThresholdProgramming}}(4, 3)$ is {\tt NP}-complete.
conclusions: $\tau$-$\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc ThresholdProgramming}}(4, 3)$ is {\tt NP}-complete
nodes.label: thm:4TP_NP-complete

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: A proof for $\tau=4$ comes first. An instance of quadripartite\footnote{The quadripartite property is not needed here, but will be so in Section~\ref{sec:complexity}.} $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$, whose {\tt NP}-completeness was proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:quad_1in3SAT}, will be reduced into an instance of $\tau$-TP(4,~3). Let us represent this instance as a pair of a set of Boolean variables $U = \{u_1, \ldots, u_n\}$ and that of clauses $C = \{c_1, \ldots, c_m\}$. Let us convert this SAT instance into a system $\mathcal{S}$ of $\tau$-inequalities with positive integer variables $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$ (needless to say, \eqref{eq:positive} is used here for their positiveness), which correspond to the SAT variables in $U$, such that the SAT instance is satisfiable if and only if the system is solvable. In $\mathcal{S}$, the $j$-th clause of $C$, $c_j = \{u_{j_1}, u_{j_2}, u_{j_3}\}$ with $1 \le j_1, j_2, j_3 \le n$, is represented as \begin{equation} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} \ge 4, v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} < 4, v_{j_1} + v_{j_3} < 4, \mbox{ and } v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} < 4, \end{equation} which is equivalent to the equation $v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} = 4$ due to the assumption that $v_{j_1}, v_{j_2}, v_{j_3} \ge 1$. Its solution must be that exactly one of the three variables is 2 and the others are 1. Therefore, if $\mathcal{S}$ is solvable, then by interpreting those in $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ with value 2 be positive and the other (that is, with value 1) negative, we can retrieve a way to satisfy the $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ instance; and vice versa. Thus, 4-TP(4, 3) is {\tt NP}-complete (in fact, we proved that even 4-TP(3, 2) is so, see \eqref{eq:clause_4}). Now the result is generalized for an arbitrary $\tau \ge 4$. In $\mathcal{S}$, we first embed systems of $\tau$-inequalities of at most three terms, presented in Section~\ref{subsec:TP_preliminaries}, that provide auxiliary variables $x_1, x_2, x_{\tau{-}4}$ with lower bounds 1, 2, and $\tau{-}4$, respectively. Combining them with an inequality \begin{equation} x_1 + x_2 + x_{\tau{-}4} < \tau \end{equation} yields $x_1 = 1$, $x_2 = 2$, and $x_{\tau{-}4} = \tau{-}4$. This means that by \eqref{eq:tau-4} being embedded, in any solution of $\mathcal{S}$, these variables must admit these respective values. Especially, the ``constant'' $x_{\tau{-}4}$ is added to the inequalities in \eqref{eq:clause_4}, and we obtain \begin{eqnarray} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} + x_{\tau{-}4} &\ge& \tau, \\ v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + x_{\tau{-}4} &<& \tau, \end{eqnarray} and the analogs of \eqref{eq:clause_lessthan_tau} for $v_{j_1} + v_{j_3}$ and $v_{j_2} + v_{j_3}$. Since $x_{\tau-4} = \tau-4$, these four $\tau$-inequalities are equivalent to $v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} = 4$. We conclude this proof by noting that any $\tau$-inequality used is either a $\ge_\tau$-inequality of at most 4 terms or a $<_\tau$-inequality of at most 3 terms, and the resulting system of $\tau$-inequalities is quadripartite. This quadripartite property will become critical in proving Theorem~\ref{thm:TC_above_4_NPhard}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce quadripartite 1-in-3-SAT: each clause becomes inequalities forcing $v_{j_1}+v_{j_2}+v_{j_3}=4$. For $\tau>4$, adders pin a constant $x_{\tau-4}=\tau-4$ added to each clause inequality.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:4TP_NP-complete} leads us to the {\tt NP}-hardness of TP. Deleting the constant term $x_{\tau-4}$ from the inequalities \eqref{eq:tau-4}, \eqref{eq:clause_atleast_tau}, and \eqref{eq:clause_lessthan_tau} yields the following inequalities: \begin{equation} x_1 + x_2 < \tau, \end{equation} \begin{equation} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} \ge \tau, v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} < \tau, v_{j_1} + v_{j_3} < \tau, \mbox{ and } v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} < \tau. \end{equation} Consider optimizing $\tau$ subject to these. Due to \eqref{eq:TP_x1x2}, the minimal possible value of $\tau$ is 4. Then its optimal value is 4 if and only if the $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ instance is satisfiable.
nodes.statement_short: Drop the constant $x_{\tau-4}$ from the Theorem 3 system; the optimum $\tau$ is 4 iff the 1-in-3-SAT instance is satisfiable.

nodes.name: Solutions with all variables below tau
nodes.statement: All the systems of $\tau$-inequalities designed in this section so far can be solved even subject to extra condition that all variables being strictly less than $\tau$. This extra condition does not prevent the systems from playing their intended roles when being embedded.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6
nodes.statement: Using this instance, now we can prove that $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc FindOptimalStrength}}$ is {\tt NP}-hard. Making use of the fact that all of its $\tau$-inequalities contain at most 4 terms, we transform them into cooperation sets of a strength-free TAS. The inequalities \eqref{eq:TP_jth_clause_lessthan_tau}, which are for the clause $c_j$, are encoded as $t_{c_j} = (v_{j_1}, v_{j_2}, v_{j_3}, x_\tau)$ with $\mathcal{D}(t_{c_j}) = \mathcal{P}(\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\}) \setminus \{\{{\tt N}\}, \{{\tt W}\}, \{{\tt S}\}, \{{\tt N}, {\tt W}\}, \{{\tt N}, {\tt S}\}, \{{\tt W}, {\tt S}\}\}$. Note that its east side is labeled with an auxiliary variable $x_\tau$, but this variable does not play any essential role but filling the blank side (the tile is not triangle but square). Likewise, the inequalities that aim at forcing $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ be positive are converted. The inequalities in \eqref{eq:positive} are encoded as a tile type $t_i = (x_1, x_a, x_\tau, x_\tau)$ with $\mathcal{D}(t_i) = \mathcal{P}(\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\}) \setminus \{\{{\tt N}\}, \{{\tt W}\}\}$. Though being not mentioned in \eqref{eq:positive}, we can assume $x_1 < \tau$ as noted in Remark~\ref{rmk:strictly_lessthan_tau}. The inequality \eqref{eq:TP_x1x2} is encoded as $t' = (x_1, x_2, x_\tau, x_\tau)$ with $\mathcal{D}(t') = \mathcal{P}(\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\}) \setminus \{\{{\tt N}\}, \{{\tt W}\}, \{{\tt N}, {\tt W}\}\}$. Then, there exists a TAS at temperature 4 that is locally equivalent to this strength-free TAS if and only if the given instance of $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ is satisfiable.
nodes.statement_short: Encode each TP(4,3) inequality group of Lemma 4's instance as the cooperation set of one tile type of a strength-free TAS.

nodes.name: Unified framework: tau-inequality system to shape
nodes.statement: We propose the following unified approach to various problems related to the behaviors and temperatures of directed TASs including the above two problems: \begin{enumerate}[Step 1.] \item choose a quadripartite system $\mathcal{S}$ of $\tau$-inequalities properly for the purpose among those built in Section~\ref{sec:behavior}; hence, all $\ge_\tau$-inequalities of $\mathcal{S}$ are of at most 4 terms and all of its $<_\tau$-inequalities are of at most 3 terms; \item convert its variables $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$ into trees of height $h$ and distinct shape, which we call {\it variable trees}, where $h$ is a parameter adjustable for our convenience; \item for each $\tau$-inequality, bundle the (at most 4) trees thus converted from its variables into a shape called the {\it logical component}; \item (two copies of) the $n$ variable trees and logical components each are mounted next to each other onto a scaffold, and amounts to a shape, which we denote by $S$. \end{enumerate}
output: a shape, which we denote by $S$
nodes.statement_short: Convert a quadripartite $\tau$-inequality system into a shape: variable trees per variable, a logical component per inequality, all mounted on a scaffold.

nodes.name: Property 1: TAS as inequality-system solver
nodes.statement: Any directed TAS $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}} = (T, \sigma, g, \tau)$ that strictly self-assembles $S$ using at most $(n + c')h + c$ tile types has (not-necessarily-distinct) $n$ glue labels $\ell_1, \ell_2, \ldots, \ell_n$ such that \begin{itemize} \item for any $m \le 4$ and $k_1, \ldots, k_m \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$, if $\mathcal{S}$ includes the $\ge_\tau$-inequality $\sum_{1 \le i \le m} v_{k_i} \ge \tau$, then $\sum_{1 \le i \le m} g(\ell_{k_i}) \ge \tau$; \item for any $m' \le 3$ and $k_1, \ldots, k_{m'} \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$, if $\mathcal{S}$ includes the $<_\tau$-inequality $\sum_{1 \le j \le m'} v_{k_j} < \tau$, then $\sum_{1 \le j \le m'} g(\ell_{k_j}) < \tau$, \end{itemize} where $c'$ is the number of $<_\tau$-inequalities in the system $\mathcal{S}$ chosen at Step 1.
assumptions: Any directed TAS $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}} = (T, \sigma, g, \tau)$ that strictly self-assembles $S$ using at most $(n + c')h + c$ tile types
conclusions: has (not-necessarily-distinct) $n$ glue labels $\ell_1, \ell_2, \ldots, \ell_n$ such that
nodes.statement_short: A small directed TAS strictly self-assembling $S$ has glue labels whose strengths satisfy the $\ge_\tau$ and $<_\tau$ inequalities of $\mathcal{S}$.
nodes.label: property:TAS_as_inequality_system_solver

nodes.name: Property 1, first item
nodes.statement: for any $m \le 4$ and $k_1, \ldots, k_m \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$, if $\mathcal{S}$ includes the $\ge_\tau$-inequality $\sum_{1 \le i \le m} v_{k_i} \ge \tau$, then $\sum_{1 \le i \le m} g(\ell_{k_i}) \ge \tau$;
assumptions: if $\mathcal{S}$ includes the $\ge_\tau$-inequality $\sum_{1 \le i \le m} v_{k_i} \ge \tau$
conclusions: then $\sum_{1 \le i \le m} g(\ell_{k_i}) \ge \tau$

nodes.name: Property 1, second item
nodes.statement: for any $m' \le 3$ and $k_1, \ldots, k_{m'} \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$, if $\mathcal{S}$ includes the $<_\tau$-inequality $\sum_{1 \le j \le m'} v_{k_j} < \tau$, then $\sum_{1 \le j \le m'} g(\ell_{k_j}) < \tau$, \end{itemize} where $c'$ is the number of $<_\tau$-inequalities in the system $\mathcal{S}$ chosen at Step 1.
assumptions: if $\mathcal{S}$ includes the $<_\tau$-inequality $\sum_{1 \le j \le m'} v_{k_j} < \tau$
conclusions: then $\sum_{1 \le j \le m'} g(\ell_{k_j}) < \tau$

nodes.name: Interpretation of Property 1
nodes.statement: This property should be interpreted that the way for the function $g$ of such a ``small'' $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ at the temperature $\tau$, if any, to assign labels with glue strengths tells how to satisfy the given system $\mathcal{S}$ of $\tau$-inequality. Conversely speaking, unless the given system admits a solution with $\tau$ being some specific value $\tau'$, any directed TAS at the temperature $\tau'$ needs strictly more than $(n+c')h+c$ tile types\footnote{ Actually, it will be proved necessary for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ to have at least $(n+c'+1)h$ tile types, which is much larger than $(n+c')h+c$ because $h \gg c_2$. } in order to strictly self-assemble $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Glue strengths of a small TAS solve the system; if the system is unsolvable at $\tau'$, any temperature-$\tau'$ TAS needs more tile types.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorems 7 and 8 via Property 1
nodes.statement: Verifying this property amounts to proofs of Theorems~\ref{thm:tau_better_than_less} and \ref{thm:TC_above_4_NPhard}; it is sufficient for us to choose a proper $\mathcal{S}$ at Step 1. In order to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:tau_better_than_less}, for $k \ge 2$, we choose the system of $\tau$-inequalities that cannot be solved for any $\tau < k$ but can for any $\tau \ge k$. This is the one designed in Section~\ref{subsec:TP_preliminaries} based on the $2^{i+1}$-adders. It is transformed into a shape $S$ through Steps 2-4. This amounts to a proof of a slightly-stronger version of Theorem~\ref{thm:tau_better_than_less}. As for Theorem~\ref{thm:TC_above_4_NPhard}, the TP instance built for Theorem~\ref{thm:4TP_NP-complete} is rather chosen. In the rest of this section, therefore, we just have to verify Property~\ref{property:TAS_as_inequality_system_solver} in order to complete the proof of these theorems.
nodes.statement_short: Instantiate the framework with the adder-based system (solvable exactly for $\tau \ge k$) for Theorem 7 and the Theorem 3 TP instance for Theorem 8; then verify Property 1.

nodes.name: variable set V
nodes.statement: Let $V = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\}$ be the set of variables occurring in the system $\mathcal{S}$ chosen at Step 1.

nodes.name: variables strictly less than tau
nodes.statement: As mentioned in Remark~\ref{rmk:strictly_lessthan_tau}, we can assume that every variable in $V$ is {\it strictly} less than $\tau$; this assumption simplifies the design of $S$ and our explanation below.

nodes.name: four-way partition of V
nodes.statement: The more essential is that $\mathcal{S}$ is quadripartite, that is to say, the variable set $V$ can be partitioned into four {\it disjoint} subsets $V_{\tt N}, V_{\tt W}, V_{\tt S}, V_{\tt E}$.
nodes.definiendum: $V_{\tt N}, V_{\tt W}, V_{\tt S}, V_{\tt E}$

nodes.name: cooperation tip
nodes.statement: This shape is a tree of height $h$ plus some constant, not depending on $h$, with only one crotch for two branches; one consists of a bit pattern and the other is of size 1 for cooperation called {\it cooperation tip}, which is numbered 1 in Figure~\ref{fig:4vars_atleast_tau}.

nodes.name: north type
nodes.statement: We say that this shape is of {\it north type} after the subscript of $V_{\tt N}$.

nodes.name: west, south and east type
nodes.statement: In this way, each variable in the other three variable subsets $V_{\tt W}, V_{\tt S}, V_{\tt E}$ is also converted into the shapes that are numbered 2, 3, 4 (and colored yellow, green, blue) in Figure~\ref{fig:4vars_atleast_tau}, respectively, and we say that these shapes are respectively of {\it west, south, and east type}.

nodes.name: variable trees
nodes.statement: All the $n$ variables of $V$ have been now associated with $n$ different tree shapes of proper type. We collectively refer to them as {\it variable trees}.

nodes.name: auxiliary trees
nodes.statement: Every conversion of $<_\tau$-inequalities in $\mathcal{S}$ into logical components at Step~3 needs to introduce an auxiliary tree of the north, west, south, or east type and recall that $\mathcal{S}$ was assumed to contain $c'$ of them (the conversion of $\ge_\tau$-inequalities does not). These trees are distinguished from each other and from the variable trees by their bit patterns.

nodes.name: tree tile-type lower bound
nodes.statement: We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ needs at least $(n+c')h$ tile types for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ to strictly self-assemble these $n+c'$ trees mainly using the results by Adleman et al.~in \cite{AdChGoHuKeEsRo2002} on tile complexity of trees.
conclusions: $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ needs at least $(n+c')h$ tile types for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ to strictly self-assemble these $n+c'$ trees

nodes.name: Proof of the tree tile-type lower bound
nodes.statement: Being duplicated, each tree has its copy that assembles upward from the scaffold (actually, all trees but at most one do so since $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ is assumed to be singly-seeded). Theorem~4.3 in \cite{AdChGoHuKeEsRo2002} implies that in order for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ to strictly self-assemble two variable trees of different types (e.g., north and west), at least $2h$ plus some constant number of tile types are necessary; $h$ exclusively for each, no matter how and at what temperature $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ is designed, where the constant is much smaller than $h$. This is not to say that $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ could not reuse any tile type for both of them. It can, for example, for their bit patterns. However, the number of such reusable tile types is bounded by a constant that is much smaller than $h$. This lower bound exists also for two trees of identical type but with distinct bit patterns. It is not allowed for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ to put tiles of identical type at the crotch positions because if they were the same, incorrect bit patterns could assemble. In contrast, $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ is able to reuse tiles of same type for the cooperation tips of these trees, but anyway it saves only one tile type. This observation is immediately generalized for more variable and auxiliary trees as: in order for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ to assemble the $n$ distinct variable trees and $c'$ auxiliary trees, at least $(n+c')h + c''$ tile types are necessary for some constant $c'' \ll h$. In brief, \[ \dtilec{\tau}(S) \ge (n+c')h + c'' \] at {\it any temperature} $\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Adleman et al.'s tree tile-complexity theorem: distinct trees (by type or bit pattern) each need about $h$ exclusive tile types.

nodes.name: same tile type at both cooperation tips
nodes.statement: Before proceeding to the explanation of next step, we prove that $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ must put the same tile type at the cooperation tip positions of two copies of each variable tree or auxiliary tree.
conclusions: $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ must put the same tile type at the cooperation tip positions of two copies of each variable tree or auxiliary tree

nodes.name: Proof that both cooperation tips carry the same tile type
nodes.statement: This is related to the position of the seed of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ so that first we see that it merely costs the number of tile types for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ to put its head on a variable tree or an auxiliary tree. Suppose $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ put its seed on one copy of some variable tree, and let us compare it with the other copy of the same tree. Recall that they are located next to each other. In order to start assembling the seed-free copy, $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ first must assemble downward from the seed and the scaffold between the copies. Then consider the process for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ to assemble the seed-free copy upward up to the counterpart position of the seed. During this process, $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ cannot reuse any tile type used for the part between the seed and scaffold; such a recycle would enable $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ to skip the assembly of the seed-free copy and produce a shape with only one copy of the variable tree. Thus, even if the seed is on a copy of some variable tree, it could not be located ``far from'' the scaffold if it were not for extra $n$ tile types available for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$. This means that $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ needs to assemble almost all parts of these trees upward, and hence, it would impose the unaffordable number of extra tile types on $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ to put tiles of distinct types at the cooperation tips of two copies of a tree.
nodes.statement_short: Counting argument on the seed's position: the seed-free copy must grow upward, and different tip tiles would cost unaffordably many extra tile types.

nodes.name: tile type t_i at cooperation tips
nodes.statement: Now, for $1 \le i \le n$, we can denote {\it the} tile type that $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ puts at the both cooperation tips of the copies of the variable tree for $v_i$ by $t_i$.

nodes.name: glue label ell_i
nodes.statement: The label $\ell_i$ mentioned in Property~\ref{property:TAS_as_inequality_system_solver} is found at the side of $t_i$ opposite to the crotch. That is, \[ \ell_i = \begin{cases} t_i({\tt S}) & \text{if $v_i \in V_{\tt N}$} \\ t_i({\tt E}) & \text{if $v_i \in V_{\tt W}$} \\ t_i({\tt N}) & \text{if $v_i \in V_{\tt S}$} \\ t_i({\tt W}) & \text{if $v_i \in V_{\tt E}$}. \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: $\ell_i$ is the glue of $t_i$ on the side opposite the crotch, chosen by the type of $v_i$'s tree.

nodes.name: logical component for a >=tau-inequality (pillars)
nodes.statement: The logical component for this $\ge_\tau$-inequality consists of the variable trees thus positioned, which we refer to as {\it pillars}, and the position adjacent to all the cooperation tips of the pillars.

nodes.name: Proof of the first item of Property 1
nodes.statement: Now we will prove the first item of Property~\ref{property:TAS_as_inequality_system_solver}, that is, if the $\ge_\tau$-inequality \begin{equation} \sum_{1 \le i \le m} v_{k_i} \ge \tau \end{equation} belongs to $\mathcal{S}$, then \begin{equation} \sum_{1 \le i \le m} g(\ell_{k_i}) \ge \tau, \end{equation} where $m \le 4$ and $k_1, \ldots, k_m \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$. Before that, however, let us quickly show that if \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_attachment} holds, then $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ can assemble the logical component for \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_inequality} by introducing only one new tile type in the following manner. $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ first assembles the respective parts of the component that correspond to the variable trees for $v_{k_1}, \ldots, v_{k_m}$ as done for the copies of these trees (hence, costs nothing) and lets their cooperation tips to cooperate to attach a tile of the new type to fill the position surrounded by the $m$ cooperation tips, which is numbered 5 in the logical component in Figure~\ref{fig:4vars_atleast_tau}. This cooperation provides enough strength for stable tile attachment due to \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_attachment}. Let us return to the proof. For the sake of contradiction, suppose \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_attachment} does not hold. Focus on the seed-free copy of the logical component for \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_inequality} for the concise argumentation. Since this copy is free from seed, $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ needs to assemble at least one pillar of the component upward from the scaffold. Under the supposition that \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_attachment} did not hold, $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ is not allowed to assemble these upward-growing pillars as done for the corresponding variable trees without any extra tile types. More precisely, at the cooperation tip of at least one of these pillars, say the one for $v_{k_i}$, $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ must put a tile of different type from $t_{k_i}$. However, this costs extra at least $h$ tile types because $\tau$ cannot reuse any tile types for the tree for $v_{k_i}$ in order to assemble this pillar, or any tile types for the any other tree $v_{k_j}$ because $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ was proved not to be able to assemble $v_{k_i}$ and $v_{k_j}$ using strictly less than $2h$ tile types (this argument works in order to prove that this pillar cannot assemble using tile types for auxiliary trees). \qed
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: if the glue sum is below $\tau$, some upward-growing pillar of the seed-free logical component needs a different tip tile, costing at least $h$ extra tile types.

nodes.name: Equation (13): >=tau inequality
nodes.statement: \sum_{1 \le i \le m} v_{k_i} \ge \tau
nodes.label: eq:at_least_tau_inequality

nodes.name: Equation (14): >=tau attachment
nodes.statement: \sum_{1 \le i \le m} g(\ell_{k_i}) \ge \tau,
nodes.label: eq:at_least_tau_attachment

nodes.name: logical component for a <tau-inequality (gadgets)
nodes.statement: Let us consider a $<_\tau$-inequality: \begin{equation} \sum_{1 \le j \le m'} v_{k_j} < \tau \end{equation} for some $m' \le 3$ and $k_1, \ldots, k_{m'} \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$. In addition to the $m'$ variable trees for $v_{k_1}, \ldots, v_{k_{m'}}$, we employ one of the $c'$ auxiliary trees prepared in Step~2 that is of distinct type from any of the variable trees (recall that $c'$ is the number of $<_\tau$-inequalities in $\mathcal{S}$). Then we combine copies of at least $m'$ of these $m'+1$ trees as done in building the components for $\ge_\tau$-inequalities but in all combinations of $m'$ trees. The combination of all the $m'+1$ trees is turned into a ``gadget'' by filling the position that are adjacent to all the cooperation tips, whereas the other combinations are considered to be gadgets without any modification. These $m'+2$ gadgets amount to the logical component for the $<_\tau$-inequality \eqref{eq:less_than_tau_inequality}, and two copies of this component are mounted on the scaffold of $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the $m'$ variable trees with a fresh auxiliary tree in all $m'$-subsets, plus the full set with its centre filled: $m'+2$ gadgets.

nodes.name: Equation (15): <tau inequality
nodes.statement: \sum_{1 \le j \le m'} v_{k_j} < \tau
nodes.label: eq:less_than_tau_inequality

nodes.name: Proof of the second item of Property 1
nodes.statement: Now we will prove that if \eqref{eq:less_than_tau_inequality} holds, then \begin{equation} \sum_{1 \le j \le m'} g(\ell_j) < \tau. \end{equation} Before this proof, let us note that since the auxiliary tree does not appear in any other component, one can have $g$ assign an arbitrary strength to the glue at the cooperation tip of this tree without causing any malfunctioning of the other component, as long as \eqref{eq:less_than_tau_attachment} holds. Setting this strength to be $\tau - \sum_{1 \le j \le m'} v_{k_j}$ enables $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ to assemble this component with introducing only one new tile type that fills the position adjacent to the cooperation tips. For the sake of contradiction, suppose that the sum $\sum_{1 \le j \le m'} g(\ell_j)$ were at least $\tau$. Focus on the seed-free copy of this component, and especially first on the gadget with $m'+1$ pillars, with the position surrouned by the cooperation tips being filled (the leftmost gadget in Figure~\ref{fig:3vars_lessthan_tau}). Let us denote this gadget by $G_1$. Due to the seed-freeness, some of the pillars of $G_1$ assemble upward and have a tile $t$ fill the position by cooperative attachment. Assume that some pillar is absent from the cooperation. Let us denote the gadget that does not contain the ``lazy'' pillar by $G_2$. Then some of the tiles put at the cooperation tips of $G_2$ must be distinct from those at the corresponding positions of $G_1$ in type in order to prevent the tile $t$ from attaching to $G_2$. However, this distinctiveness would cost $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ extra $h$ new tile types, as explained in the proof of the first item. Thus, all of the pillars of $G_1$ must join the cooperation, and hence, all the pillars of $G_1$ assemble upward. Then consider the gadget that is free from the auxiliary pillar, which we denote by $G_3$. The types of tiles at the corresponding cooperation tips of $G_1$ and $G_3$ must be the same in order for $\ensuremath{\mathcal{T}}$ not to pay the unaffordable extra $h$ tile types. However, then there must exist $1 \le j \le m'$ such that the tile $t_j$ at the cooperation tip of the tree for $v_j$ and the tile at the corresponding position in $G_1$ must differ from each other in type because of the supposition $\sum_{1 \le j \le m'} g(\ell_j) \ge \tau$. This again causes the unaffordable cost. Consequently, we can say that \eqref{eq:less_than_tau_attachment} must hold. \qed
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: if the glue sum reaches $\tau$, comparing gadgets $G_1$, $G_2$, $G_3$ forces some differing tip tile, again costing $h$ extra tile types.

nodes.name: Equation (16): <tau attachment
nodes.statement: \sum_{1 \le j \le m'} g(\ell_j) < \tau.
nodes.label: eq:less_than_tau_attachment

nodes.name: the constant c
nodes.statement: As the readers might have already noticed, the constant $c$ is the numbers of tile types for the scaffold (actually, equal to its length, which depends only on the number of variables and the number of inequalities in $\mathcal{S}$) plus the number of tile types for each variable tree that exceeds $h$ (top structures differ tree by tree, but a bit).

nodes.name: Non-monotonicity of directed tile complexity
nodes.statement: There exists a shape $S$ such that $\dtilec{3}(S) < \dtilec{4}(S)$.
conclusions: There exists a shape $S$ such that $\dtilec{3}(S) < \dtilec{4}(S)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.statement: As explained into details when being introduced, the framework needs only our appropriate choice of a system of $\tau$-inequalities at Step 1. Actually, it suffices to find as such a system the one that is solvable for $\tau = 3$ but not for $\tau = 4$. Such an equation, however, was already given as \eqref{eq:TP_example_1} in Section~\ref{subsec:TP_preliminaries}. Needless to say, all $\ge_\tau$-inequalities and all $<_\tau$-inequalities in this system are of at most 4 and 3 terms, respectively, and this system is quadripartite.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the unified framework to system (1), which separates temperatures 3 and 4.

nodes.name: Strictly decreasing tile complexity
nodes.statement: A problem of theoretical interest is whether for any temperature $\tau$, there exists a shape $S$ such that $\dtilec{k}(S)$ is strictly decreasing over the interval $[1, \tau]$.

nodes.name: Unbounded tile-complexity ratio at arbitrary temperature
nodes.statement: As for Theorem~\ref{thm:tau_better_than_less}, our interest lies on the ratio $\dtilec{< \tau}(S_\tau)/\dtilec{\tau}(S_\tau)$. In our construction of $S_\tau$, the ratio is constant no matter how $h$ is adjusted. In contrast, $\dtilec{1}(\square{n})/\dtilec{2}(\square{n})$ can get arbitrarily large by making $n$ larger, provided the conjecture $\dtilec{1}(\square{n}) = 2n-1$ is true (or even $\dtilec{1}(\square{n}) = \Omega(n)$ is fine). Can we find such a shape for arbitrary temperature?
nodes.statement_short: Is there, for every temperature, a shape whose tile-complexity ratio between lower temperatures and $\tau$ is unbounded?

nodes.name: Set up the inequality system of a single tile with full coop
nodes.statement: In order to see this, let us consider a simple strength-free TAS with only one tile type $t = (\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3, \ell_4)$ and a cooperation set $\mathcal{D}(t) = \{\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\}\}$. Finding a TAS at lowest temperature that is locally equivalent to this strength-free TAS is equal to solving the following system of inequalities with a {\it positive integer} variable $\tau$: \begin{equation} \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} \ell_1 + \ell_2 + \ell_3 + \ell_4 &\ge& \tau \\ \ell_1 + \ell_2 + \ell_3 &<& \tau \\ \ell_1 + \ell_2 + \ell_4 &<& \tau \\ \ell_1 + \ell_3 + \ell_4 &<& \tau \\ \ell_2 + \ell_3 + \ell_4 &<& \tau \\ \end{array} \right. \end{equation} so as to minimize $\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the inequality system of a single tile with full cooperation set

nodes.name: Minimum temperature of this system is 4
nodes.statement: The minimum $\tau$ for this system is 4 with $\ell_1 = \ell_2 = \ell_3 = \ell_4 = 1$ (with $\tau$ being strictly less than 4, this system is not solvable).
nodes.statement_short: Minimum temperature of this system is 4

nodes.name: Inequalities correspond to (non-)members of the cooperation
nodes.statement: The first inequality in \eqref{eq:TP_example_1} corresponds to $\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\} \in \mathcal{D}(t)$, the second corresponds to $\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}\} \not\in \mathcal{D}(t)$, and so forth. Though \eqref{eq:TP_example_1} does not seem to contain an inequality corresponding to $\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}\} \not\in \mathcal{D}(t)$, the second one (or third) actually implies this, and hence, not presented for the sake of space. In any case, the system for a cooperation set contains at most 15 inequalities.
nodes.statement_short: Inequalities correspond to (non-)members of the cooperation set; at most 15 needed

nodes.name: Set up a reduction from monotone 1-in-3-SAT
nodes.statement: Let us denote a given instance of monotone $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ by a pair of a set $U$ of Boolean variables and a set of clauses of three literals, which are positive due to the monotonicity. We will show a polynomial-time reduction from this to an instance of quadripartite $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up a reduction from monotone 1-in-3-SAT

nodes.name: Plan: replace each clause by a quadripartite conjunction
nodes.statement: The reduction first transforms each clause of the given $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ instance into a quadripartite conjunction of clauses while preserving the $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ satisfiability, and then conjuncts them. Each conjunction is designed so that it admits a partition of its variables into four disjoint sets one of which contains all variables of its source clause.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: replace each clause by a quadripartite conjunction

nodes.name: Define the 13-clause gadget (5) for each clause
nodes.statement_short: Define the 13-clause gadget (5) for each clause

nodes.name: Claim: the gadget preserves 1-in-3 satisfiability, by cases
nodes.statement: We claim that this preserves the $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ satisfiability. If the $i$-th clause is $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ satisfied, then due to the symmetry among $x, y, z$ in \eqref{eq:quad_1in3SAT_conjunction}, it suffices to examine the case $x = 1, y = z = 0$. Then this conjunction is $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ satisfied by setting $a_1, d_x, e_{yz}, f_{xy}, f_{zx}$ to be 1 and the others to be 0. If $x = y = z = 0$, then the first three clauses in \eqref{eq:quad_1in3SAT_conjunction} imply $a_1 = a_2 = a_3 = 0$, but then the fourth clause cannot be satisfied. In the case $x = y = 1$, we consider two cases depending on the value of $c$. If $c = 0$, then $d_x = d_y = 1$ must hold in order to satisfy $\{\neg x, c, d_x\}$ and $\{\neg y, c, d_y\}$, but then the clause $\{d_x, d_y, e_{xy}\}$ contains too many true variables. Otherwise, $d_x = d_y = e_{xy} = 0$, but then the clause cannot be satisfied. Therefore, the clause $\{x, y, z\}$ is $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ satisfiable if and only if so are all clauses in \eqref{eq:quad_1in3SAT_conjunction}.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: the gadget preserves 1-in-3 satisfiability, by cases on $x,y,z$

nodes.name: Case exactly one true: explicit satisfying assignment
nodes.statement: If the $i$-th clause is $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ satisfied, then due to the symmetry among $x, y, z$ in \eqref{eq:quad_1in3SAT_conjunction}, it suffices to examine the case $x = 1, y = z = 0$. Then this conjunction is $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ satisfied by setting $a_1, d_x, e_{yz}, f_{xy}, f_{zx}$ to be 1 and the others to be 0.
nodes.statement_short: Case exactly one true: explicit satisfying assignment

nodes.name: Case all false: fourth clause fails
nodes.statement: If $x = y = z = 0$, then the first three clauses in \eqref{eq:quad_1in3SAT_conjunction} imply $a_1 = a_2 = a_3 = 0$, but then the fourth clause cannot be satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Case all false: fourth clause fails

nodes.name: Case two true: both values of $c$ lead to contradiction
nodes.statement: In the case $x = y = 1$, we consider two cases depending on the value of $c$. If $c = 0$, then $d_x = d_y = 1$ must hold in order to satisfy $\{\neg x, c, d_x\}$ and $\{\neg y, c, d_y\}$, but then the clause $\{d_x, d_y, e_{xy}\}$ contains too many true variables. Otherwise, $d_x = d_y = e_{xy} = 0$, but then the clause cannot be satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Case two true: both values of $c$ lead to contradiction

nodes.name: Subcase $c=0$

nodes.name: Reduce quadripartite 1-in-3-SAT to 4-TP(4,3)
nodes.statement: A proof for $\tau=4$ comes first. An instance of quadripartite\footnote{The quadripartite property is not needed here, but will be so in Section~\ref{sec:complexity}.} $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$, whose {\tt NP}-completeness was proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:quad_1in3SAT}, will be reduced into an instance of $\tau$-TP(4,~3). Let us represent this instance as a pair of a set of Boolean variables $U = \{u_1, \ldots, u_n\}$ and that of clauses $C = \{c_1, \ldots, c_m\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce quadripartite 1-in-3-SAT to 4-TP(4,3)

nodes.name: Encode each clause as inequalities (7), equivalent to sum =
nodes.statement: Let us convert this SAT instance into a system $\mathcal{S}$ of $\tau$-inequalities with positive integer variables $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$ (needless to say, \eqref{eq:positive} is used here for their positiveness), which correspond to the SAT variables in $U$, such that the SAT instance is satisfiable if and only if the system is solvable. In $\mathcal{S}$, the $j$-th clause of $C$, $c_j = \{u_{j_1}, u_{j_2}, u_{j_3}\}$ with $1 \le j_1, j_2, j_3 \le n$, is represented as \begin{equation} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} \ge 4, v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} < 4, v_{j_1} + v_{j_3} < 4, \mbox{ and } v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} < 4, \end{equation} which is equivalent to the equation $v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} = 4$ due to the assumption that $v_{j_1}, v_{j_2}, v_{j_3} \ge 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Encode each clause as inequalities (7), equivalent to sum = 4

nodes.name: Solutions correspond to 1-in-3 assignments (value 2 = true)
nodes.statement: Its solution must be that exactly one of the three variables is 2 and the others are 1. Therefore, if $\mathcal{S}$ is solvable, then by interpreting those in $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ with value 2 be positive and the other (that is, with value 1) negative, we can retrieve a way to satisfy the $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ instance; and vice versa.
nodes.statement_short: Solutions correspond to 1-in-3 assignments (value 2 = true)

nodes.name: Conclude NP-completeness for $\tau = 4$
nodes.statement: Thus, 4-TP(4, 3) is {\tt NP}-complete (in fact, we proved that even 4-TP(3, 2) is so, see \eqref{eq:clause_4}).
nodes.statement_short: Conclude NP-completeness for $\tau = 4$

nodes.name: Embed adders and inequality (8) to pin $x_{\tau-4} = \tau-4$
nodes.statement: Now the result is generalized for an arbitrary $\tau \ge 4$. In $\mathcal{S}$, we first embed systems of $\tau$-inequalities of at most three terms, presented in Section~\ref{subsec:TP_preliminaries}, that provide auxiliary variables $x_1, x_2, x_{\tau{-}4}$ with lower bounds 1, 2, and $\tau{-}4$, respectively. Combining them with an inequality \begin{equation} x_1 + x_2 + x_{\tau{-}4} < \tau \end{equation} yields $x_1 = 1$, $x_2 = 2$, and $x_{\tau{-}4} = \tau{-}4$. This means that by \eqref{eq:tau-4} being embedded, in any solution of $\mathcal{S}$, these variables must admit these respective values.
nodes.statement_short: Embed adders and inequality (8) to pin $x_{\tau-4} = \tau-4$

nodes.name: Add the constant to clause inequalities, giving (9)-(10)
nodes.statement: Especially, the ``constant'' $x_{\tau{-}4}$ is added to the inequalities in \eqref{eq:clause_4}, and we obtain \begin{eqnarray} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} + x_{\tau{-}4} &\ge& \tau, \\ v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + x_{\tau{-}4} &<& \tau, \end{eqnarray} and the analogs of \eqref{eq:clause_lessthan_tau} for $v_{j_1} + v_{j_3}$ and $v_{j_2} + v_{j_3}$. Since $x_{\tau-4} = \tau-4$, these four $\tau$-inequalities are equivalent to $v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} = 4$.
nodes.statement_short: Add the constant to clause inequalities, giving (9)-(10)

nodes.name: All inequalities are TP(4,3) and the system is quadripartite
nodes.statement: We conclude this proof by noting that any $\tau$-inequality used is either a $\ge_\tau$-inequality of at most 4 terms or a $<_\tau$-inequality of at most 3 terms, and the resulting system of $\tau$-inequalities is quadripartite. This quadripartite property will become critical in proving Theorem~\ref{thm:TC_above_4_NPhard}.
nodes.statement_short: All inequalities are TP(4,3) and the system is quadripartite

nodes.name: Delete the constant term to obtain (11)-(12)
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:4TP_NP-complete} leads us to the {\tt NP}-hardness of TP. Deleting the constant term $x_{\tau-4}$ from the inequalities \eqref{eq:tau-4}, \eqref{eq:clause_atleast_tau}, and \eqref{eq:clause_lessthan_tau} yields the following inequalities: \begin{equation} x_1 + x_2 < \tau, \end{equation} \begin{equation} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} \ge \tau, v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} < \tau, v_{j_1} + v_{j_3} < \tau, \mbox{ and } v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} < \tau. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Delete the constant term to obtain (11)-(12)

nodes.name: Inequality (11) forces $\tau \ge 4$
nodes.statement: Consider optimizing $\tau$ subject to these. Due to \eqref{eq:TP_x1x2}, the minimal possible value of $\tau$ is 4.
nodes.statement_short: Inequality (11) forces $\tau \ge 4$

nodes.name: Optimum is 4 iff the instance is satisfiable
nodes.statement: Then its optimal value is 4 if and only if the $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc 1-in-3-\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc Sat}}}}$ instance is satisfiable.
nodes.statement_short: Optimum is 4 iff the instance is satisfiable

nodes.name: Plan: turn each inequality group into a cooperation set
nodes.statement: Using this instance, now we can prove that $\ensuremath{\mbox{\sc FindOptimalStrength}}$ is {\tt NP}-hard. Making use of the fact that all of its $\tau$-inequalities contain at most 4 terms, we transform them into cooperation sets of a strength-free TAS.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: turn each inequality group into a cooperation set

nodes.statement: The inequalities \eqref{eq:TP_jth_clause_lessthan_tau}, which are for the clause $c_j$, are encoded as $t_{c_j} = (v_{j_1}, v_{j_2}, v_{j_3}, x_\tau)$ with $\mathcal{D}(t_{c_j}) = \mathcal{P}(\{{\tt N}, {\tt W}, {\tt S}, {\tt E}\}) \setminus \{\{{\tt N}\}, \{{\tt W}\}, \{{\tt S}\}, \{{\tt N}, {\tt W}\}, \{{\tt N}, {\tt S}\}, \{{\tt W}, {\tt S}\}\}$. Though being not mentioned in \eqref{eq:positive}, we can assume $x_1 < \tau$ as noted in Remark~\ref{rmk:strictly_lessthan_tau}.

nodes.statement_short: Tile $t'$ encodes (11)

nodes.statement: Verifying this property amounts to proofs of Theorems~\ref{thm:tau_better_than_less} and \ref{thm:TC_above_4_NPhard}; it is sufficient for us to choose a proper $\mathcal{S}$ at Step 1.

This is the one designed in Section~\ref{subsec:TP_preliminaries} based on the $2^{i+1}$-adders. It is transformed into a shape $S$ through Steps 2-4. This amounts to a proof of a slightly-stronger version of Theorem~\ref{thm:tau_better_than_less}.

nodes.statement: As for Theorem~\ref{thm:TC_above_4_NPhard}, the TP instance built for Theorem~\ref{thm:4TP_NP-complete} is rather chosen.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 8: use the Theorem 3 TP instance
